strengths: The paper is well-grounded in cognitive neuroscience, successfully integrating the theory of brain predictive coding into an fMRI-to-text decoding framework.
The proposed PREDFT model demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on the Narratives dataset, outperforming the strong UniCoRN baseline across various sequence lengths.

The paper includes outstanding analytical experiments, such as verifying the predictive coding hypothesis in fMRI data, analyzing the spatial specificity of predictive coding regions (ROIs), and exploring optimal predictive distances.

The decoding error analysis (Appendix B) provides a highly insightful discussion of how discrete sampling (TR) in fMRI leads to information loss at the end of frames, and how the predictive side network successfully mitigates this.
weaknesses: The evaluation is limited to a single dataset (Narratives). Testing on other naturalistic language fMRI datasets would better demonstrate the generalizability of the proposed framework.
The absolute performance for higher-order n-grams (BLEU-2/3/4) remains very low, reflecting the general difficulty of fMRI-to-text reconstruction, which could be discussed further.

The model architecture is relatively complex and depends on sensitive hyperparameters (such as lambda and the cross-attention mask design) that vary with the sequence length, which might affect generalizability and ease of reproduction.

strengths: Strong cognitive and neuroscientific motivation: The paper is well-grounded in the theory of predictive coding. Instead of blindly applying a deep learning model, the authors first verify the predictive coding hypothesis in the fMRI data and identify specific regions of interest (ROIs) to guide their model design.

Innovative architecture: The proposed PREDFT model effectively uses a dual-network approach (main decoder network and side predictive coding network) to fuse future-oriented brain representations into the translation/decoding pipeline through cross-attention.

Rigorous methodology and data handling: The authors adopt a strict leak-free cross-subject split on the Narratives dataset to ensure realistic generalization and fair comparison, avoiding common data leakage pitfalls in fMRI-to-text literature.

Insightful decoding error analysis: The paper includes a very compelling analysis of positional decoding errors, shedding light on how the discrete sampling rate (TR) of fMRI leads to information loss for words occurring later in the interval, and how the side network successfully mitigates this limitation.
weaknesses: Limited baseline comparison: The model is primarily compared against a single strong baseline (UniCoRN). Additional baseline models, even simpler sequence-to-sequence networks or standard autoregressive models without side networks, would make the empirical comparison more robust.

Evaluation on only a single dataset: Although Narratives is currently the largest naturalistic language comprehension fMRI dataset, validating the model on a second dataset (e.g., Pereira) would significantly strengthen the claims of generalizability.

Low absolute reconstruction quality: While PREDFT achieves state-of-the-art results, the absolute metrics (e.g., very low BLEU-2/3/4 scores) show that generating fluent and semantically precise text from fMRI remains an open challenge, as shown in the case studies where decoded sentences are still highly fragmented.

strengths: Addresses a highly challenging and exciting interdisciplinary task: reconstructing continuous natural language from non-invasive fMRI brain recordings.
Well-motivated by the cognitive neuroscience theory of 'predictive coding', translating this concept into a dual-network architecture with a main decoding network and an auxiliary side network.
Includes several interesting analytical experiments, such as exploring the effect of different brain regions (ROIs), analyzing prediction distances, and discussing temporal information loss in fMRI.
weaknesses: Extremely weak baseline comparison. The proposed model is only compared against a single baseline (UniCoRN). The exclusion of other prominent state-of-the-art frameworks (e.g., Tang et al., 2023; Ye et al., 2023) is justified only by 'incompatible settings,' which is scientifically insufficient; these baselines should be adapted and re-evaluated under the same split/preprocessing conditions.

Very poor generation quality and limited evaluation metrics. The absolute reconstruction quality is extremely low (BLEU-4 scores are mostly under 1%, and BLEU-2 scores are under 9%). The case study shows that the generated text is largely ungrammatical and incoherent. Standard MT metrics like BLEU/ROUGE are poorly suited for evaluating such noisy generation; semantic-level evaluations (e.g., BERTScore, GPT-based evaluations, or brain-decoding identification accuracy) are missing.

The connection to neuroscience is somewhat oversold. Computationally, the 'brain predictive coding' side network functions simply as a standard future-token prediction multi-task regularizer. The claim of modeling 'brain predictive coding' would be much stronger if the authors demonstrated that this specifically aligns with human neural prediction mechanisms compared to standard language model future-token prediction.
The figures in the paper (especially Figures 1, 2, and 6) are very difficult to read. They suffer from extremely small fonts, overlapping text labels, and poor contrast.

The paper lacks details and methodology on how it addresses inter-subject variability during cross-subject decoding. Performing cross-subject fMRI decoding without anatomical/functional alignment usually explains the exceptionally poor generation quality, and this limitation is not sufficiently addressed.

strengths: Strong and elegant grounding in neuroscientific theory (predictive coding), connecting brain prediction mechanisms directly to fMRI-to-text decoding architectures.

Well-designed model architecture (PREDFT) which employs a side-network specifically focused on predicting future word representations, leveraging a custom masked attention mechanism for seamless integration into the main decoding network.
Comprehensive empirical validation across two major naturalistic language comprehension datasets (LeBel's and Narratives), consistently outperforming strong state-of-the-art baselines.

Thorough and insightful analyses, including the verification of predictive coding in different ROIs, spatial/temporal scale analysis (prediction distance and length), and an interesting discussion on mitigating fMRI information loss due to discrete temporal sampling.
weaknesses: While the proposed method significantly outperforms baselines, the absolute performance of open-vocabulary fMRI decoding remains very low (e.g., BLEU-4 is often under 2.0%), illustrating the extreme difficulty of the task.

The definition and formulation in the Predictive Coding Verification section (Section 2) could be clearer regarding how $X \oplus X^d_l$ is constructed, shaped, and fed into the ridge regression model.

Some critical model details (like the FIR model details and specific ROI parcellation indices) are heavily delegated to the appendix, which slightly hurts the flow of reading the main methodology section.

strengths: Strong cognitive neuroscience motivation, successfully translating predictive coding theory (how the human brain naturally predicts future linguistic contents) into a practical fMRI-to-text decoding architecture.
Comprehensive and rigorous preliminary experiments validating the predictive coding hypothesis in both LeBel's and Narratives datasets before model construction.

Superior decoding performance compared to existing state-of-the-art baselines (including MapGuide, BrainLLM, and UniCoRN) across multiple evaluation metrics in both within-subject and cross-subject settings.

Excellent analytical experiments, including the investigation of different brain regions (BPC, Whole, Random), the impact of prediction length/distance, and a detailed positional decoding error analysis showing how the side network alleviates information loss.
weaknesses: The BLEU-3 and BLEU-4 scores across all models remain extremely low (often below 2%), indicating that while the proposed method improves over baselines, reconstructing exact continuous n-grams from fMRI remains highly challenging, and word-level overlap metrics might not fully capture semantic recovery.
The model architecture is relatively complex and computationally heavier during training, requiring the joint optimization of two parallel network structures (main and side networks).

strengths: The concept of integrating predictive coding theory from cognitive neuroscience to guide fMRI-to-text decoding is creative and intellectually interesting.
The paper evaluates the model on two popular datasets (LeBel's and Narratives) with both within-subject and cross-subject configurations.
weaknesses: A major concern is the extremely high performance of the chance-level baseline (where fMRI images are randomly shuffled), which achieves around 20% BLEU-1 (Tables 6 and 7). This strongly suggests that the evaluation is heavily dominated by the language model's prior or that there is significant data leakage/overlap between the train and test stimuli, making the absolute performance improvements difficult to trust.

The neuroscientific explanation for the 'information loss' in Section D and Figure 13 is biophysically flawed. The authors claim that because of discrete fMRI sampling (TR), the first few words are recorded while the latter words in a TR are 'lost'. In reality, the BOLD response is a sluggish hemodynamic signal that acts as a low-pass filter, integrating neural activity over several seconds. Blurring occurs, but not a selective loss of the end of the TR. The higher error rate at the end of a sequence is a well-documented phenomenon in auto-regressive seq2seq generation (compounding errors) rather than fMRI sampling. A text-only control is needed to back up this claim.

The selected 'BPC' (Brain Predictive Coding) ROIs (STS, IFG, SMG, Angular Gyrus, Broca's area) are simply the standard language network. Showing that using these language regions yields better decoding than random regions or the whole brain (which includes visual/motor noise) is expected and does not specifically validate the predictive coding hypothesis over general language localization.

The evaluation metrics are highly unstable. In Table 1, the ROUGE1-R for 'PREDFT w/o SideNet' on Sub-2 is 50.28% but drops to 24.90% for the full 'PREDFT' model, while ROUGE1-P increases from 17.41% to 38.43%. Such massive fluctuations make it difficult to conclude that the side network systematically improves translation quality rather than just shifting the precision/recall trade-off of an unstable generator.

The qualitative results in Table 8 show that the decoded language remains highly incoherent and resembles 'word salad' (e.g., 'He don’t know my girl you of the eyes...'). The automatic metrics (especially BLEU-1) are likely inflated by high-frequency unigrams.

There are multiple writing errors and incorrect figure citations. For example, Section 2 refers to 'results shown in Figure 12' on page 2, but Figure 12 is in the appendix on page 17 and only shows $l=2$, whereas the text is discussing findings across multiple prediction lengths $l$ (which are actually in Figure 9).
